Accuser of the Brethren
uh-KYOO-zer uhv thuh BREH-thrin
noun (a title of Satan)
From Latin accusare, to call to account; rendering the Greek kategor, a prosecutor in a court; brethren from Old English brothor, the saints as brothers in Christ.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Accuser of the Brethren is a title of Satan, the great adversary whose office is to slander and indict the people of God. John hears in heaven a loud voice proclaiming, "Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night" (Rev 12:10). The pattern is set early: in Job, Satan presents himself before the LORD and slanders the patriarch's integrity (Job 1:9-11); in Zechariah he stands at the right hand of Joshua the high priest to resist him, and is rebuked, "The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan" (Zech 3:2). His Greek name diabolos means slanderer. Against this ceaseless accusation stands the believer's mighty comfort: Christ is the Advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1), and Paul asks, "Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth" (Rom 8:33). This dictionary confesses that the accusations of the devil, though often true of our sin, are silenced by the imputed righteousness of Christ, who answers every charge at the bar of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A title of Satan as the slanderer who indicts the saints before God day and night. His every accusation is answered by Christ the Advocate and the justifying verdict of the Father.

expand to see more

ACCUSER OF THE BRETHREN, noun. A scriptural title of Satan, the adversary who slanders and brings charges against the people of God.

He accuses the saints before the throne day and night, as in the visions of Job, Zechariah, and the Revelation.

"The accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night" (Rev 12:10).

His office requires of the saint no self-defence but flight to the Advocate, and forbids despair under his charges.

His sentence is already pronounced: cast down, and to be cast at last into the lake of fire.

📖 Key Scripture

Rev 12:10 — "And I heard a loud voice saying in heaven, Now is come salvation, and strength, and the kingdom of our God, and the power of his Christ: for the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night."

Job 1:9 — "Then Satan answered the LORD, and said, Doth Job fear God for nought?"

Zech 3:1 — "And he shewed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to resist him."

1 John 2:1 — "My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous:"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the danger is the modern denial of a personal devil, which leaves the conscience defenceless before its own accusations.

expand to see more

The modern temper, embarrassed by a personal devil, reduces the accuser to a psychological projection or an inner voice of guilt. But Scripture knows a real adversary, a created spirit fallen into malice, who stands before God to indict the saints. To deny him is not to be rid of his accusations but to be left without the doctrine that answers them.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the courtroom of grace: the elect have an Advocate, and the Judge who would condemn is the very God who justifies. Whatever the accuser charges, true or false, the blood of Christ and His imputed righteousness silence the prosecution forever.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek kategor (accuser) and diabolos (slanderer), the legal vocabulary of Satan's office against the saints.

expand to see more

Kategor, Greek, a prosecutor or accuser, used of Satan in Revelation 12:10.

Diabolos, Greek, slanderer or false accuser, the common New Testament name for the devil.

Satan, Hebrew, the adversary, the one who opposes and resists.

Advocate, Greek parakletos, one called alongside to plead, the office of Christ for His own.

The courtroom imagery of Job, Zechariah, and Romans frames sin as a charge and grace as the verdict.

Usage

"When the accuser of the brethren whispered his old sins, the believer fled to the Advocate and was at peace."

"The pastor preached that the accuser's charges are often true, but always answered in Christ."

"Luther taught the saint to send the accuser of the brethren to the cross, where every debt is paid."
